key_results: Secs. 1.3-1.3.1 (physical PDF pp. 31-35; printed pp. 8-12): a signal bandlimited to fmax is determined by samples at fs >= 2fmax; 2fmax is the Nyquist rate and fs/2 the Nyquist frequency.

Secs. 1.3.2-1.3.3 (physical PDF pp. 35-38; printed pp. 12-15): real signals require an analog antialias prefilter, while processing hardware imposes the complementary upper bound; a feasible design must satisfy 2fmax <= fs <= fproc.

Sec. 1.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 39-41; printed pp. 16-18): sampled sinusoids whose analog frequencies differ by integer multiples of fs have identical samples; ideal reconstruction selects the unique alias in [-fs/2, fs/2].

Secs. 1.5.1-1.5.2 (physical PDF pp. 46-51; printed pp. 23-28): the DTFT is periodic with fs in physical-frequency units, and sampling replicates the analog spectrum at every integer multiple of fs according to the Poisson summation formula.

Secs. 1.6.1-1.6.3 (physical PDF pp. 58-70; printed pp. 35-47): ideal reconstruction is sinc interpolation; a zero-order hold adds half-sample linear phase and sinc-amplitude droop, which may be digitally equalized before an analog postfilter removes images.

Sec. 1.7 (physical PDF pp. 70-73; printed pp. 47-50): a practical DSP chain separates five roles: analog antialias prefilter, A/D converter, digital processor, D/A converter (optionally equalized), and analog anti-image postfilter.

Sec. 2.1 (physical PDF pp. 86-94; printed pp. 63-71): for a B-bit uniform converter of full-scale range R, Q=R/2^B; rounded error lies in [-Q/2,Q/2], and under the busy-signal model it has mean zero, variance Q^2/12, and RMS Q/sqrt(12).

Sec. 2.1 (physical PDF pp. 94-98; printed pp. 71-75): quantizer dynamic range grows by approximately 6B dB; the additive-white-noise model is useful for wide-amplitude, rapidly varying signals but fails visibly for small or slowly varying inputs.

Sec. 2.2 (physical PDF pp. 98-104; printed pp. 75-81): unshaped oversampling by L gains one-half effective bit per doubling, whereas pth-order noise shaping makes the asymptotic gain (p+1/2)log2(L), minus an order-dependent constant.

Secs. 2.3-2.4 (physical PDF pp. 104-111; printed pp. 81-88): successive-approximation A/D conversion needs B binary-search decisions for B bits; a counter may need up to 2^B steps, while a flash converter trades speed for 2^B-1 parallel comparators.

Sec. 2.5 (physical PDF pp. 111-116; printed pp. 88-93): nonsubtractive triangular dither is the practical all-purpose choice for decorrelating quantization error; subtractive rectangular dither makes error independent without an SNR penalty but requires reproducing the same dither at decoding.
Secs. 3.2-3.3 (physical PDF pp. 123-130; printed pp. 100-107): an LTI system is completely characterized by its impulse response, and its output is the convolution y(n)=sum_k h(k)x(n-k).

Secs. 3.4-3.5 (physical PDF pp. 130-138; printed pp. 107-115): FIR systems have finite impulse responses and can be nonrecursive; IIR systems have infinite responses and commonly use feedback difference equations. Causality is h(n)=0 for n<0, and BIBO stability is equivalent to absolute summability of h.

Sec. 3.5 (physical PDF pp. 138-140; printed pp. 115-117): a stable anticausal tail may be clipped before -D and delayed to obtain a practical causal approximation; for |x(n)|<=A, the error is bounded by A times the discarded absolute tail.

Secs. 4.1.1-4.1.6 (physical PDF pp. 145-158; printed pp. 122-135): convolving lengths Lx and Lh gives length Lx+Lh-1, and direct, tabular, LTI, Toeplitz-matrix, and flip-and-slide forms are algebraically identical views of the same operation.

Secs. 4.1.7 and 4.1.10 (physical PDF pp. 158-167; printed pp. 135-144): finite convolution naturally splits into input-on transient, steady overlap, and input-off transient; overlap-add extends block convolution to very long or unbounded streams by summing shifted block outputs.

Secs. 4.3.2-4.3.4 (physical PDF pp. 178-188; printed pp. 155-165): a real-time FIR filter is a dot product against a tapped delay line; updating the state in the wrong order destroys needed samples, while circular buffering changes a pointer instead of shifting the entire state.

Secs. 5.1-5.3 (physical PDF pp. 214-223; printed pp. 191-200): linearity, delay, and convolution map naturally into z-domain algebra, but a rational expression is not a complete transform without its ROC; causal, anticausal, and two-sided sequences occupy exterior, interior, and annular ROCs.

Sec. 5.3 (physical PDF pp. 221-223; printed pp. 198-200): stability requires the ROC to contain the unit circle; therefore a stable causal rational system has all poles inside it, while a stable anticausal system has all poles outside it.

Sec. 5.4 (physical PDF pp. 223-231; printed pp. 200-208): the DTFT is X(z) evaluated on z=exp(jomega); Parseval equates time-domain energy with integrated spectral energy, and pole/zero distances give a geometric construction of magnitude and phase.

Sec. 5.5 (physical PDF pp. 231-237; printed pp. 208-214): partial fractions recover a rational sequence only after the ROC chooses the right- or left-sided term associated with each pole; among the admissible ROCs, exactly one containing the unit circle yields the stable inverse.

Sec. 5.6 (physical PDF pp. 237-242; printed pp. 214-219): the unilateral z-transform incorporates initial conditions directly and converts causal recurrences into algebraic equations without separately adding a zero-input response.

Secs. 6.1-6.2 (physical PDF pp. 248-252; printed pp. 225-229): transfer function, frequency response, realization, difference equation, pole-zero pattern, impulse response, and convolution equation are seven equivalent filter descriptions; design proceeds from desired H(omega) to H(z) to a realization.
Sec. 6.3.1 (physical PDF pp. 252-255; printed pp. 229-232): complex sinusoids are LTI eigenfunctions, so the steady-state response multiplies amplitude by |H(omega)| and adds phase arg H(omega).

Sec. 6.3.2 (physical PDF pp. 255-260; printed pp. 232-237): switching on a sinusoid adds pole-governed transients; if rho is the largest pole magnitude, an epsilon settling estimate is neff=ln(epsilon)/ln(rho), exposing the cost of poles close to the unit circle.

Sec. 6.4.2 (physical PDF pp. 263-270; printed pp. 240-247): a conjugate pole pair at radius R and angle omega0 creates a resonator with approximate 3-dB width Delta omega approximately 2(1-R); narrower bandwidth therefore means slower transient decay.

Secs. 6.4.2-6.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 267-274; printed pp. 244-251): paired pole-zero sections create boost, cut, or notch equalizers, while arbitrary harmonic combs place unit-circle zeros at rejection frequencies and slightly contracted poles at the same angles to control width.

Sec. 6.5 (physical PDF pp. 274-283; printed pp. 251-260): inverse filtering swaps zeros and poles; zeros outside the unit circle force a stable inverse to be anticausal, and delayed truncation can make it implementable, but inversion may amplify measurement noise severely.

Secs. 7.1-7.2 (physical PDF pp. 294-306; printed pp. 271-283): direct form II commutes numerator and denominator subfilters and merges their equal delay chains, reducing storage from separate input/output histories to K=max(M,L) delays.

Sec. 7.3 (physical PDF pp. 306-309; printed pp. 283-286): transposing a signal-flow graph reverses branches, swaps inputs and outputs, and preserves the transfer function; transposed structures can improve overflow and coefficient-quantization behavior.
Sec. 7.4 (physical PDF pp. 309-317; printed pp. 286-294): for s(n+1)=As(n)+Bx(n), y(n)=Cs(n)+Dx(n), H(z)=C(zI-A)^(-1)B+D and h(n)=CA^(n-1)B u(n-1)+D delta(n); transposition maps A,B,C to A^T,C^T,B^T.

Secs. 7.5-7.6 (physical PDF pp. 317-329; printed pp. 294-306): real rational filters decompose into first- and second-order cascade sections, but pole-zero pairing and section ordering are not unique and materially affect finite-precision noise and overflow.

Sec. 7.7 (physical PDF pp. 329-340; printed pp. 306-317): circular buffers make delay-line maintenance constant-cost; an FIR of order M needs roughly M+1+C instructions per sample and a K-biquad IIR roughly 5K+C, turning instruction time into a maximum real-time fs.

Secs. 8.1-8.3 (physical PDF pp. 355-363; printed pp. 332-340): lattice/ladder filters realize rational H(z) using reflection coefficients gamma and ladder taps; normalized sections use tau=sqrt(1-gamma^2), keep internal branch gains below unity, and improve roundoff/overflow robustness.

Sec. 8.4 (physical PDF pp. 363-370; printed pp. 340-347): forward and backward Levinson recursions map denominator coefficients to and from reflection coefficients, while a corresponding triangular recursion maps the numerator into ladder coefficients.

Sec. 8.7 (physical PDF pp. 374-376; printed pp. 351-353): the Schur-Cohn criterion gives a recursion-only stability test: a causal polynomial denominator is stable iff every extracted reflection coefficient satisfies |gamma_p|<1.

Secs. 8.9-8.10 (physical PDF pp. 377-383; printed pp. 354-360): roots of high-order direct-form polynomials can move dramatically under small coefficient perturbations, especially when clustered; cascade or normalized-lattice realizations retain stability much better in the book's quantization experiments.

Sec. 9.1 (physical PDF pp. 385-394; printed pp. 362-371): multiplying by a finite record window convolves the ideal spectrum with the window spectrum, replacing lines by mainlobes and sidelobes; for a rectangular length-L record, resolvability requires Delta f >= fs/L.

Sec. 9.1 (physical PDF pp. 389-391; printed pp. 366-368): a Hamming window suppresses first sidelobes from 13.26 dB to about 42.67 dB but roughly doubles mainlobe width; resolution lost to a wider window can be recovered only with a longer record.

Secs. 9.2-9.3 (physical PDF pp. 395-401; printed pp. 372-378): the DTFT is a polynomial evaluated on the unit circle and may be computed at selected frequencies by Horner's rule; two lines are resolved when separated by roughly the window's 3-dB width, but a weak line also must exceed leakage from stronger neighbors.

Sec. 9.3 (physical PDF pp. 399-401; printed pp. 376-378): the DPSS window maximizes energy concentration inside a prescribed mainlobe band, while the Dolph-Chebyshev window minimizes mainlobe width for a prescribed equal-sidelobe level.

Sec. 9.6 (physical PDF pp. 418-423; printed pp. 395-400): the ordinary periodogram is asymptotically unbiased but inconsistent because its variance does not vanish; averaging K segment periodograms typically reduces variance by K, at the cost of shorter-segment resolution.

Sec. 9.6 (physical PDF pp. 422-423; printed pp. 399-400): Welch uses usually 50%-overlapping segments; lag-window smoothing instead windows the sample autocorrelation, which convolves and smooths the ordinary periodogram in frequency.

Sec. 9.7 (physical PDF pp. 424-426; printed pp. 401-403): a strictly stable LTI filter maps a WSS input PSD to Syy(omega)=|H(omega)|^2 Sxx(omega); for white input, the noise-reduction ratio is sigma_y^2/sigma_x^2=integral |H|^2 d omega/(2pi)=sum_n h(n)^2.

Sec. 9.7 (physical PDF pp. 425-426; printed pp. 402-403): an ideal accumulator driven by white noise is a nonstationary random walk with variance (n+1)sigma_x^2; moving the pole to rho<1 creates a leaky integrator and restores strict stability.

For a length-L record x(n), the N-point DFT is the DTFT sampled at ω_k=2πk/N: X_k=X(ω_k). The record length L and transform length N are conceptually independent; X_k is periodic in k with period N, negative-frequency bins wrap to N−k, and a real record gives conjugate symmetry X_{N−k}=X_k*. [§10.1]

Zero padding changes only the density of frequency samples on the same underlying DTFT; it does not add physical information or improve the ability to separate tones. Padding in front of a record additionally imposes linear phase, whereas padding at the end does not. [§§10.2–10.3]

Physical resolution is controlled by observation length, Δf_phys≈f_s/L, while the plotted/computational bin spacing is Δf_comp=f_s/N. Increasing N interpolates the spectrum; increasing L narrows the record-window main lobe and can genuinely resolve nearby sinusoids. [§10.3, Examples 10.3.1–10.3.2]

If L>N, modulo-N reduction wraps x(n) into an N-point sequence by summing samples whose indices differ by N; the N-point DFT of that wrapped sequence equals the N samples of the original DTFT. This makes aliasing in time the dual of sampling in frequency. [§10.5, Eqs. 10.5.1–10.5.5]

The DFT matrix is unitary up to scale: the inverse transform uses the conjugate kernel and factor 1/N. Orthogonality of roots of unity supplies both inversion and Parseval-style energy identities. [§§10.4, 10.6]

The radix-2 FFT factors an N-point DFT into even- and odd-index N/2-point transforms with twiddle factors; recursive decimation reduces arithmetic from order N² to order N log₂N and leads to the butterfly signal-flow graph and bit-reversed indexing. [§10.8]

DFT multiplication implements modulo-N circular convolution. It equals ordinary linear convolution when the transform length is at least the output length (for a length-L input and order-M FIR, N≥L+M); shorter N aliases the linear-convolution tail back into the beginning. [§§10.9–10.10]

Overlap-add partitions the input into blocks, linearly convolves each with the FIR, then adds the M-sample overlaps; overlap-save processes overlapping N-sample input blocks and discards the first M corrupted samples. Both turn long filtering into repeated FFT products. [§10.11]

Window-method FIR design starts from the inverse DTFT d(k) of an ideal response, truncates or tapers it, then shifts it to make a causal length-N filter. A symmetric impulse response has exact linear phase and constant group delay M=(N−1)/2. [§§11.1.1–11.1.3]

Rectangular truncation of a jump discontinuity produces Gibbs ripples whose maximum overshoot approaches Si(π)/π−1/2=0.08949; increasing N squeezes them toward the discontinuity but does not reduce their height. A Hamming taper reduces maximum overshoot to about 0.2% at the price of a wider transition. [§§11.1.2–11.2, Eq. 11.2.6]

The Kaiser window supplies an adjustable ripple/transition tradeoff through shape α and length N. Its empirical design equations translate stopband/passband ripple and transition width into α and N−1=Df_s/Δf; among the compared windows it is near-optimal in sidelobe energy and simple to implement. [§11.3.1, Eqs. 11.3.7–11.3.11, Table 11.3.1]

A linear-phase highpass complement can be constructed from a lowpass design by H_HP(z)=z^{−M}−H_LP(z); the responses sum to a pure delay. The same complementarity supports crossover networks and multiband graphic equalizers without redesigning every band independently. [§11.3.1, Eqs. 11.3.16–11.3.17]

For spectral analysis, the record window convolves the line spectrum with the window transform. Rectangular windows have a narrow main lobe but about −13 dB sidelobes; Hamming gives roughly −40 dB; Kaiser lets the sidelobe level be selected. Record length controls main-lobe separation, while sidelobe attenuation controls whether weak tones near strong ones remain visible. [§11.3.2]

The frequency-sampling FIR method approximates the inverse-DTFT integral by an inverse N-point DFT of desired frequency samples and can then window the resulting impulse response; it makes explicit that frequency samples alone specify a periodic/interpolated response between grid points only through the chosen construction. [§11.4]

The bilinear map s=(1−z^{−1})/(1+z^{−1}) maps the stable left half of the s-plane into the unit disk and the imaginary axis onto the unit circle. Its nonlinear frequency map Ω=tan(ω/2) requires prewarping but preserves stability and avoids frequency aliasing. [§12.1, Eqs. 12.1.3–12.1.8]

Lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and bandstop variants of the bilinear transformation let one start from an analog lowpass prototype. First- and second-order sections obtain exact prescribed cutoff, center-frequency, bandwidth, Q, and reference-gain conditions by solving those conditions in the prewarped analog domain. [§§12.1–12.6]

Second-order peaking and notch designs place the prescribed center exactly and define bandwidth at an arbitrary reference gain G_B, not only the 3-dB level. Complementary peak/notch pairs and the substitution z→z^D extend the same construction to periodic combs. [§§12.3, 12.5]

Parametric equalizers are specified directly by center frequency, bandwidth, reference gain, and boost/cut gain; shelving variants control the low- or high-frequency plateau, and the prescribed-Nyquist-gain form removes an otherwise hidden endpoint constraint. [§§12.4–12.4.2]

An Nth-order Butterworth lowpass has maximally flat squared magnitude 1/[1+(Ω/Ω_0)^{2N}]. Stable factors are obtained by selecting the left-half-plane poles; after prewarping and bilinear transformation, lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and bandstop digital designs are implemented as cascades of first- and second-order sections. [§§12.7–12.11]

Chebyshev type I filters concentrate equiripple error in the passband and type II in the stopband. The order follows from the passband/stopband ripple ratio and frequency ratio via inverse hyperbolic cosine, and the pole/zero formulas again lead naturally to cascaded sections. [§12.12]

Butterworth, Chebyshev I, Chebyshev II, and elliptic lowpass filters share |H(Ω)|²=1/[1+ε_p²F_N²(Ω/Ω_p)] and a degree equation F_N(k^{−1})=k_1^{−1}, where k=Ω_p/Ω_s and k_1=ε_p/ε_s. This unifies order selection and makes the selectivity/discrimination tradeoff explicit. [§13.1, Eqs. 13.1.3–13.1.9]

Elliptic (Cauer/Zolotarev) filters are equiripple in both passband and stopband and achieve the smallest order for fixed brick-wall specifications, but have the most nonlinear passband phase among the compared classical types. In the chapter’s common example the required orders are Butterworth 35, either Chebyshev 10, and elliptic 5. [§13.1, Figs. 13.1.2–13.1.3]

The elliptic characteristic is built from Jacobian cd functions; the elliptic degree equation relates the complete elliptic integrals for k and k_1 to N. Landen transformations provide a rapidly convergent computational route for evaluating the functions and solving the degree equation. [§§13.2–13.4]

Analog elliptic design obtains zeros and poles by mapping the rational characteristic into the s-plane, then normalizes and pairs conjugates into stable real sections. The same framework degenerates cleanly to Butterworth and both Chebyshev families. [§§13.5–13.7]

Lowpass prototypes can be converted to analog or digital highpass, bandpass, and bandstop filters by pole/zero and frequency-specification transformations. Frequency-shifted digital realizations replace each unit delay in a lowpass section by a second-order allpass-like mapping to translate a lowpass band into a chosen bandpass or bandstop interval. [§§13.8–13.13]

An L-fold interpolator first inserts L−1 zeros between samples and then uses a lowpass FIR to remove the L−1 intermediate spectral images. The ideal filter passes the original baseband with gain L and cutoff equal to the old Nyquist frequency f_s/2, expressed on the new Lf_s clock. [§§14.1–14.2.3]

The interpolation filter splits into L polyphase subfilters D_i(z), each operating at the original low rate and producing one phase of the L output samples. This is algebraically equivalent to high-rate convolution but avoids multiplying by inserted zeros and reduces work by about L. [§14.2.2, Eqs. 14.2.11–14.2.15]

Kaiser interpolation designs choose the transition around f_s/2 and stop the nearest image; multistage factorizations L=L_0L_1… replace one extremely sharp high-rate filter with a cascade whose early filters run slowly and whose later transitions are wider. [§§14.2.4–14.2.5]

Hold and linear interpolation are short, inexpensive filters with characteristic droop. Their simple time-domain rules illuminate how polyphase branches calculate the missing samples, while later digital equalizers can compensate DAC and postfilter passband loss. [§§14.1, 14.3–14.4.5]

Decimation requires lowpass filtering before taking every Lth sample so that shifted spectral copies do not overlap. Oversampling widens the analog antialias/anti-image transition bands, shifting the difficult selectivity from analog hardware into digital interpolation and decimation filters. [§14.5]

A rational sample-rate change L/M is implemented by interpolation by L followed by decimation by M; the two lowpass filters can be combined, and a polyphase schedule computes only outputs that survive downsampling. The text’s canonical audio conversion is 44.1 kHz↔48 kHz, requiring 160/147 or 147/160. [§14.6]

In a first-order delta-sigma ADC model, H_x(ζ)=ζ^{−1} and H_NS(ζ)=1−ζ^{−1}: the desired input is delayed but otherwise unchanged, while quantization noise is highpass-shaped out of baseband before decimation. A pth-order shaper uses H_NS(ζ)=(1−ζ^{−1})^p. [§14.7, Eqs. 14.7.3–14.7.12]

Noise-shaping requantization for DACs applies the same feedback principle after interpolation: fewer retained bits create more quantization noise, but the loop pushes it outside baseband for the analog postfilter to remove. This is the chapter’s precise form of trading bits for samples. [§14.7, Eqs. 14.7.14–14.7.15]

For additive x=s+v, perfect undistorted extraction requires H=1 wherever S is nonzero and H=0 wherever V is nonzero, which is possible only when signal and noise spectra do not overlap. Otherwise filter design is necessarily a distortion-versus-noise compromise. [§15.1, Eqs. 15.1.1–15.1.4]

For white input noise, the noise-reduction ratio is R=σ_y²/σ_v²=∑_n h_n²=(1/2π)∫|H(ω)|²dω. An ideal lowpass of width ω_c gives R=ω_c/π, and if the signal is passed unchanged then SNR_out/SNR_in=1/R. [§15.1, Eqs. 15.1.5–15.1.8]

The unity-DC exponential moving average H(z)=(1−λ)/(1−λz^{−1}) has R=(1−λ)/(1+λ) and effective ε-settling time n_eff=ln ε/ln λ. Moving λ toward one improves noise suppression by narrowing the passband, but lengthens the transient. [§15.2]

The optimum length-N FIR smoother under unity-DC-gain and minimum white-noise NRR has equal coefficients 1/N and R=1/N. Compared at equal R it settles faster than the EMA, but costs N MACs rather than two; its linear-phase group delay is (N−1)/2. [§15.5, Eqs. 15.5.3–15.5.6]

Phase delay controls carrier shift, while group delay controls a narrowband envelope’s shift. Increasing selectivity pushes poles toward the unit circle and generally increases NRR performance, settling time, and group delay together; the experiments turn this into a three-way design tradeoff rather than a single attenuation target. [§§15.7–15.9]

SMA and EMA smoothers lag trends; predictive moving-average (PMA) and double-EMA (DEMA) combinations can cancel nominal lag and estimate slope, but their noise reduction is weaker. The chapter treats lag, prediction horizon, transient length, and NRR as coupled metrics. [§15.10]

The substitution z→z^D replicates a single lowpass peak or highpass notch D times around the unit circle. Complementary periodic comb and notch filters have |H_comb|²+|H_notch|²=1, prescribed peak/notch width up to π/D, and preserve NRR under the replication because zeros inserted into h(n) do not change ∑h_n². [§15.11, Eqs. 15.11.3–15.11.14]

For NTSC-style composite video, line- or frame-delay combs exploit the deliberate 180° subcarrier phase reversal to separate interleaved luminance and chrominance spectra. A line comb is motion-robust but loses vertical detail; a frame comb separates more exactly only for nearly static images. Complementary lowpass/bandpass filtering can reinsert the lost vertical detail. [§15.12]

A causal sinusoid can be generated as the impulse response of a second-order resonator; combining sine and cosine sections into the coupled form uses only the pole components a and b rather than a²+b², improving coefficient quantization. Periodic waveforms are impulse responses of N(z)/(1−z^(−D)), while a wavetable and circular pointer provide the lower-overhead realization. [§§16.1.1–16.1.3, Eqs. 16.1.1–16.1.22]

Adding a delayed copy gives the FIR comb H(z)=1+az^(−D), with spectral peaks separated by fs/D; feeding the delayed output back gives the IIR comb H(z)=1/(1−az^(−D)). Its epsilon-level decay time is neff=D ln(epsilon)/ln(a), or tau_eff=TD ln(epsilon)/ln(a). [§16.2.1, Eqs. 16.2.1–16.2.16]

Flanging and chorusing are time-varying delay effects: y(n)=x(n)+a x(n−d(n)). Short periodic delay modulation moves the comb notches; chorusing uses a nonzero base delay and often several independently modulated voices, whereas phasing realizes moving notches with time-varying allpass sections. [§16.2.2, Eq. 16.2.17 and surrounding algorithms]

A realistic reverberator separates direct sound, sparse early reflections, and dense late reflections. Schroeder structures build density from comb/allpass sections; putting a lowpass G(z) in the feedback loop makes high-frequency poles shorter and their transients decay faster, with approximate pole radius |G(omega_i)|^(1/D). Stability is guaranteed by |G(omega)|<1. [§16.2.3, Eqs. 16.2.32–16.2.39]

The Karplus–Strong plucked-string model initializes a delay line with noise and recirculates it through G(z)=(1+z^(−1))/2. Choosing D≈fs/f1 fixes pitch, while repeated lowpass passes make high frequencies decay faster in a natural string-like way. [§16.2.3, Eq. 16.2.40]

Compressor/expander gain is driven by a smoothed level c_n=lambda c_(n−1)+(1−lambda)|x_n|, with lambda=epsilon^(Ts/t_eff). Piecewise power-law gain functions implement compression or expansion above/below a threshold; limiters and gates are extreme ratios. [§§16.3.1–16.3.2, Eqs. 16.3.1–16.3.8]

Separate attack and release constants are obtained by switching lambda according to whether the detected level rises or falls. Smoothing the nonlinear gain and optionally delaying the signal suppresses overshoot; a side-chain supports ducking and filtered side-chains support de-essing. [§16.3.3, Eqs. 16.3.9–16.3.13]

A high-order peaking equalizer is obtained by designing a Butterworth, Chebyshev-1, Chebyshev-2, or elliptic analog lowpass shelf and applying s=(1−2 cos(omega0)z^(−1)+z^(−2))/(1−z^(−2)). The mapping sends equalizer bandedges to ±Omega_B and turns analog order N into digital order 2N. [§§17.1–17.2, Eqs. 17.2.2–17.2.18]

The prototype magnitude |Ha|²=(G²+G0² epsilon² FN²)/(1+epsilon² FN²) meets bandwidth gain GB when epsilon=sqrt((G²−GB²)/(GB²−G0²)). Choosing left-half-plane roots makes the design minimum phase, so equal-and-opposite boost and cut designs are exact inverses when their gain specifications are reciprocals. [§§17.2–17.4 and §17.6, Eqs. 17.2.10–17.2.16 and 17.6.5–17.6.7]

When both passband and secondary stopband widths are specified, Butterworth and Chebyshev order formulas follow directly from the normalized bandwidth and gain ratios, while the elliptic order uses quarter-period ratios and is rounded upward; the rounding slightly improves one specification. [§17.5, Eqs. 17.5.1–17.5.5]

Digital octave bandwidth is warped and generally asymmetric around a high center frequency. The exact equation is solved by a rapidly convergent iteration initialized by B≈(omega0/sin omega0)b; a separate remapping lets the designer state a conventional 3-dB width while retaining Chebyshev/elliptic ripple specifications. [§17.6, Eqs. 17.6.8–17.6.15]

Frequency-shifted transposed, normalized-lattice, and minimum-noise state-space realizations expose different numerical tradeoffs. The latter two have scaling and roundoff advantages for low center frequencies or rapidly varying parameters; weighted-arithmetic-mean bandwidth permits a fully decoupled realization whose gain, bandwidth, and center-frequency coefficients are independently controlled. [§§17.7–17.8, Eqs. 17.7.1–17.8.8]

In time-varying equalizer tests, transposed, normalized-lattice, and state-space forms remain comparable while the canonical form develops large oscillations from unscaled states. Turning gain on gradually removes overshoot; the text recommends the transposed form as a strong cost/robustness compromise. [§17.9, Figs. 17.9.6–17.9.7]

The STFT forms overlapping length-N frames separated by hop R, windows each, and computes an N-point DFT. For input length Lx, M=floor(Lx/R) and zero extension to MR+N gives M+1 complete frames; spectrogram axes are f_k=kfs/N and t_m=mR/fs. [§§18.2–18.3, Eqs. 18.2.1–18.3.1]

Inverse-frame division by a small window is numerically unsafe. Overlap-add instead yields y(n)=x(n) w_tilde(n); exact reconstruction divides by the overlapped window, while the COLA condition W(2pi r/R)=0 for r=1,…,R−1 makes w_tilde constant. [§18.4, Eqs. 18.4.1–18.4.6]

An STFT processing system may use distinct analysis and synthesis hops: analyze, transform X_km into Y_km, inverse-transform, apply a synthesis window, and overlap-add. The middle transform can implement filtering, denoising, gain control, fading, or phase modification. [§§18.5–18.6, Eqs. 18.5.1–18.6.4]

The phase vocoder preserves STFT magnitudes but estimates each bin's instantaneous-frequency offset from the modulo-2pi phase increment, Delta omega=(1/Ra)[Phi_km−Phi_k,m−1−Ra omega_k]_mod2pi, then advances synthesis phase by Rs(omega_k+Delta omega). [§§18.7 and 18.9, Eqs. 18.7.1–18.7.3 and 18.9.8–18.9.10]

Time-scale modification follows from the hop ratio r=Ra/Rs: duration changes while phase propagation preserves frequency content. Pitch scaling without duration change composes resampling with reciprocal phase-vocoder time scaling; pitch scaling is multiplicative f→rf, not additive frequency translation. [§§18.8–18.10, Eq. 18.8.1 and Fig. 18.10.1]

The normalized type-2 DCT is an orthogonal matrix transform D=Ax with inverse x=A^T D and Parseval identity ||x||²=||D||². Even extension converts it to a 2N-point FFT, yielding a fast forward and exactly reversible inverse algorithm. [§19.2, Eqs. 19.2.1–19.2.15]

DCT compression works because smooth signal blocks concentrate energy into relatively few coefficients. One method keeps a fixed count of largest coefficients per frame; another zeros every coefficient below a global fraction of the maximum. The true storage cost must include coefficient locations as well as values. [§19.3, Eqs. 19.3.1–19.3.2]

The MDCT maps 2N samples to N coefficients and is not invertible on one block: its IMDCT returns antisymmetrized/symmetrized half-blocks. With 50% overlap, the alias term from one block has the opposite sign in the next, so overlap-add cancels it and recovers the shared N samples exactly. [§19.4, Eqs. 19.4.1–19.4.8]

A symmetric length-2N analysis/synthesis window preserves TDAC when w_n²+w_(n+N)²=2 in the book's normalization. Sine and Vorbis windows satisfy this directly; cumulative sums of a symmetric seed window generate a general family including the KBD window used in AAC and AC-3. [§19.5, Eqs. 19.5.1–19.5.8]

The complete MDCT compression chain is 50%-overlapped framing, Princen–Bradley windowing, MDCT thresholding, IMDCT, a second window, and overlap-add. Boundary samples require padding or special handling because only interior half-blocks participate in TDAC. [§19.6, Eq. 19.6.10]

A multiresolution analysis is a nested sequence V_j whose orthonormal basis functions are scaled/translated copies phi_jn(t)=2^(j/2)phi(2^j t−n). A finite-resolution signal decomposes into one coarse projection plus mutually orthogonal detail spaces, and the mapping from finest samples to coarse/detail coefficients is the DWT. [§20.1, Eqs. 20.1.1–20.1.16]

Nesting V_j inside V_(j+1) forces two-scale dilation equations for the scaling and wavelet functions. Their filter coefficients h and g generate the analysis/synthesis relations that underlie Mallat's pyramid; choosing g as the conjugate mirror of h supplies the orthogonal detail branch. [§20.2, Eqs. 20.2.1–20.2.14]

Orthonormality requires even-shift correlations equal to Kronecker deltas and the quadrature identity |H(omega)|²+|H(omega+pi)|²=2. Daubechies D_K filters have length 2K and K Nyquist zeros; equivalently the wavelet has K vanishing moments and annihilates polynomials through degree K−1. [§20.3, Eqs. 20.3.1–20.3.20]

Mallat analysis filters with time-reversed lowpass/highpass filters and downsamples; synthesis upsamples and filters with h and g. Downsampling aliases each subband, but the quadrature conditions make the complete two-channel bank perfectly reconstructing. [§20.4, Eqs. 20.4.4–20.4.15]

The periodized DWT can be expressed as an orthogonal matrix w=W^T x, x=Ww, or as circular-convolution filter-bank stages. It stores exactly N coefficients and costs O(MN), linear in signal length for fixed filter order M; package outputs can differ by signs and cyclic shifts without representing a different transform. [§20.5, Eqs. 20.5.1–20.5.23]

Wavelet denoising transforms, thresholds only detail coefficients, and inverts. Hard thresholding deletes small coefficients; soft thresholding also shrinks survivors and is the exact solution of an L2 data-fit plus L1 wavelet penalty. VisuShrink uses lambda=sigma sqrt(2 log2 N), with sigma estimated robustly from finest-scale details. [§20.7, Eqs. 20.7.1–20.7.8]

The undecimated wavelet transform removes all downsamplers and instead uses successively dilated à-trous filters. It is redundant and costs O(N log N), but remains perfectly reconstructing through the half-sum identity and is shift invariant; the source's benchmark shows better denoising than the ordinary DWT. [§20.8, Eqs. 20.8.1–20.8.8 and Fig. 20.8.6]

For a continuous-time transfer function with direct feedthrough, initial conditions immediately before and after t=0 need not agree. Up to second order, y(0+)=y(0−)+b0x(0+) and y_dot(0+)=y_dot(0−)+b0x_dot(0+)+(b1−a1b0)x(0+); these mappings reconcile Laplace zero-input/zero-state and classical homogeneous/forced solutions. [§§21.2–21.4, Eqs. 21.2.1–21.4.4]

Forward Euler, backward Euler, and trapezoidal discretization are one substitution family s=(1−z^(−1))/(p+qz^(−1)): (p,q)=(0,T), (T,0), and (T/2,T/2). Substituting into Ha(s) gives explicit first- and second-order coefficient maps. [§21.8, Eqs. 21.8.1–21.8.5]

Zero-order hold is Hd(z)=(1−z^(−1)) Z{Ha(s)/s}; first-order hold is Hd(z)=((1−z^(−1))²/(Tz^(−1))) Z{Ha(s)/s²}. Partial fractions turn these definitions into exact pole mappings z=e^(pT) and implementable first-/second-order difference equations. [§21.9, Eqs. 21.9.1–21.9.15]

Real-time implementation iterates the difference equation sample by sample. For a second-order system initialized from continuous-time conditions, y_(−1)≈y(0−) and y_(−2)≈y(0−)−T y_dot(0−); a third-order initialization also uses T² y_double_dot(0−). [§§21.7 and 21.10–21.11, Eqs. 21.7.3–21.7.8]

The zero-order hold is step invariant: the digital step response equals samples of the analog step response. Its impulse response equals the integral of h_a over the preceding sample interval; conventional impulse invariance h_d(n)≈T h_a(nT) is only a small-T approximation and needs a half-weight correction at n=0 for causal discontinuities. [§§21.14–21.15, Eqs. 21.14.14–21.15.5]

First-order hold linearly interpolates the input over each sampling interval and is ramp invariant. For a pure integrator, ZOH reduces to forward Euler while FOH reduces to the trapezoidal rule, unifying the hold and numerical-integration viewpoints. [§§21.16–21.17, Eqs. 21.16.1–21.17.1]

For negative feedback with plant G and controller Gc, the reference, error, and disturbance paths share denominator 1+GcG: H=GcG/(1+GcG), Herr=1/(1+GcG), and Hdist=G/(1+GcG). This makes tracking, disturbance rejection, and closed-loop pole placement one algebraic problem. [§22.1, Eqs. 22.1.2–22.1.3]

A PID controller Gc=kp+ki/s+kd s trades rise time, overshoot, and settling time. The final-value theorem exposes steady-state error; in the presented plants a nonzero integral term is required for zero step and ramp tracking error. [§22.2, Eqs. 22.2.1–22.2.2]

A digital loop must include the hold-plus-plant equivalent Gd(z), not merely substitute z into the analog closed loop. A practical digital PID uses trapezoidal integration and backward-Euler differentiation: kp+(kiT/2)(1+z^(−1))/(1−z^(−1))+(kd/T)(1−z^(−1)). [§22.3, Eqs. 22.3.1–22.3.4]

The examples progress from linear cruise and antenna plants to an inverted pendulum and a genuinely nonlinear on/off thermostat. The thermostat is simulated by forward time stepping with a discontinuous furnace control R(n)=R0 when T(n)<Tc(n), showing why a difference equation can be more useful than a closed-form transfer function. [§§22.4.1–22.4.4, Eqs. 22.4.29–22.4.35]

Local polynomial smoothing fits y≈Sc by least squares, giving c=(S^T S)^(−1)S^T y and fitted samples y_hat=By with B=S(S^T S)^(−1)S^T. B is a symmetric idempotent orthogonal projector; its columns are position-specific smoothing filters that handle the two boundaries without padding. [§§23.2–23.4, Eqs. 23.2.2–23.2.16]

The central filter is simultaneously the least-squares polynomial fit and the minimum-noise-reduction-ratio filter subject to moment constraints sum n^i b(n)=delta_i. Those constraints preserve polynomial inputs and signal moments through degree d and are equivalent to d derivatives of a flat frequency response at DC. [§23.8, Eqs. 23.8.1–23.8.21]

Evaluating the fitted polynomial away from the center yields predictive/interpolating FIR filters; differentiating it yields minimum-norm derivative filters. A Farrow structure factors the continuously variable delay parameter into polynomial powers while fixed subfilters process the samples. [§§23.6–23.7 and 23.9, Eqs. 23.6.1–23.9.11]

Higher polynomial degree preserves more high-frequency detail but passes more noise: asymptotically the quadratic/cubic and quartic/quintic central filters have NRR about 2.25/N and 3.52/N, versus 1/N for the averager. [§23.8, Eqs. 23.8.2–23.8.3]

Weighted local polynomial fits lead to minimum-roughness filters when the quadratic noise metric is prefiltered by a difference operator D(z)=(1−z^(−1))^s. Henderson filters and Hahn orthogonal polynomials provide closed, computationally stable representations of this family. [§§23.11–23.13, Eqs. 23.11.1–23.11.30]

Missing samples and known outliers are handled by assigning them zero weight, estimating them from surrounding samples, and then smoothing the adjusted record. Robust filtering automates this with iterated bisquare weights derived from median-scaled residuals; 3–4 iterations are usually adequate. [§23.15, Eqs. 23.15.1–23.15.10]

For unequally spaced observations, a local bandwidth h_t selects neighbors and a compact window weights them; the local weighted normal equations return value, slope, and higher derivatives. Fixed bandwidth keeps h constant while nearest-neighbor bandwidth keeps the local sample count constant, exposing the bias–variance tradeoff directly. [§23.16, Eqs. 23.16.1–23.16.28]

Leave-one-out cross-validation can be computed without N refits: x_hat_(−i)=(x_hat_i−H_ii y_i)/(1−H_ii), so CV averages ((y_i−x_hat_i)/(1−H_ii))². GCV replaces H_ii by tr(H)/N; both are useful guides but the ethanol example shows their optimum may visibly undersmooth. [§23.17, Eqs. 23.17.1–23.17.9; §23.18, Figs. 23.18.4–23.18.5]

Adaptive local polynomial smoothing estimates normalized curvature and shrinks bandwidth where curvature is high, preserving benchmark peaks and discontinuities that a fixed bandwidth broadens. Repeated observations are exactly reducible to their average with the local weight multiplied by their multiplicity; LOESS adds nearest-neighbor tricube fits and iterative robustness weights. [§§23.19–23.21, Eqs. 23.19.1–23.21.2]

Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1184-1188; printed pp. 1161-1165): the steady EMA update a_n=lambda a_(n-1)+(1-lambda)y_n is a predictor/corrector whose constant gain retains the ability to track changing means, unlike the running mean's gain 1/(n+1), which vanishes.

Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1186-1188; printed pp. 1163-1165): for white observation noise, EMA NRR is (1-lambda)/(1+lambda), effective lag is lambda/(1-lambda), and matching both to an N-point SMA gives lambda=(N-1)/(N+1).

Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1187-1188; printed pp. 1164-1165): for any unity-DC-gain filter, effective lag is sum_n n h_n, equivalently minus H'(1)/H(1) and the group delay at DC; smaller variance necessarily trades against slower response.

Sec. 24.2 (physical PDF pp. 1192-1193; printed pp. 1169-1170): EMA is the optimal one-step predictor for an IMA(1,1), or ARIMA(0,1,1), process; it is also the steady Kalman predictor for a random-walk state observed in white noise, with q=sigma_w^2/sigma_v^2=alpha^2/(1-alpha).

Secs. 24.3-24.4 (physical PDF pp. 1193-1198; printed pp. 1170-1175): weighted local-polynomial smoothing solves c=(S^TWS)^(-1)S^TWy; estimates at offset tau are linear filters whose moments exactly reproduce every polynomial of degree at most d.

Sec. 24.4 (physical PDF pp. 1196-1198; printed pp. 1173-1175): the order-1 predictive FIR filter is the minimum-NRR length-N filter constrained to unity DC gain and lag -tau; tau=0 yields local level, its derivative channel yields local slope, and tau=1 gives the next-sample forecast.

Secs. 24.5-24.6 (physical PDF pp. 1198-1209; printed pp. 1175-1186): high-order EMA admits an exact RLS-like recursion for polynomial state, gain, and inverse covariance; its large-time limit becomes a fixed-gain state-space smoother realizable by a cascade of identical first-order EMAs.

Secs. 24.8-24.10 (physical PDF pp. 1214-1219; printed pp. 1191-1196): twicing H into 2H-H^2 cancels first-order passband error and always produces zero DC lag; repeated residual correction gives 1-(1-H)^(d+1), while general Kaiser-Hamming sharpening can improve both passband and stopband orders.

Sec. 24.10 (physical PDF pp. 1217-1219; printed pp. 1194-1196): zero lag in a causal smoother requires negative impulse-response coefficients and commonly creates a passband peak just above DC; delay reduction is therefore not free.

Secs. 24.11-24.13 (physical PDF pp. 1219-1227; printed pp. 1196-1204): cascaded outputs of any unity-gain lowpass filter can be linearly combined into local level, slope, and acceleration estimates using its first two moments; Holt generalizes the level/slope gains independently, and Holt-Winters adds a D-period seasonal state.

Sec. 25.2 (physical PDF pp. 1233-1235; printed pp. 1210-1212): SMA, WMA, TMA, EMA, and ILRS filters are compared by the same two invariants, NRR=sum h_n^2 and lag=sum n h_n; increasing span reduces noise but increases decision delay.

Sec. 25.3 (physical PDF pp. 1235-1237; printed pp. 1212-1214): the predictive moving average h_tau minimizes NRR subject to unity gain and lag -tau; ordinary SMA and WMA emerge as tau=-(N-1)/2 and tau=-(N-1)/3 special cases.

Sec. 25.11 (physical PDF pp. 1265-1274; printed pp. 1242-1251): volatility bands differ chiefly in their center and width estimators; parabolic SAR is a time-varying EMA of the current trend's extreme price whose gain increases on new extremes and resets when price crosses the stop.

Sec. 25.14 (physical PDF pp. 1282-1293; printed pp. 1259-1270): Markowitz portfolio selection is a linearly constrained quadratic minimization; its risk-return efficient frontier is parabolic, adding a risk-free asset creates a tangent capital asset line whose slope is the maximum Sharpe ratio, and CAPM makes excess return proportional to beta.

Secs. 26.1-26.2 (physical PDF pp. 1294-1299; printed pp. 1271-1276): smoothing splines balance weighted interpolation error against integrated derivative energy; the equally spaced Whittaker-Henderson analogue minimizes ||y-x||_W^2+lambda||D_s x||_2^2 and has solution x=(W+lambda D_s^T D_s)^(-1)Wy.

Sec. 26.2 (physical PDF pp. 1297-1299; printed pp. 1274-1276): D_s^T D_s is sparse and banded with width 2s+1, making global smoothing efficient; GCV provides an automatic lambda criterion but often undersmooths and must be checked visually or against domain constraints.

Sec. 26.3 (physical PDF pp. 1300-1302; printed pp. 1277-1279): the infinite-record WH smoother has H(omega)=1/[1+lambda|D(omega)|^2]; for s differences, H=1/[1+lambda|2sin(omega/2)|^(2s)] and the complementary residual filter is 1-H.

Sec. 26.4 (physical PDF pp. 1302-1305; printed pp. 1279-1282): the s=2 Hodrick-Prescott smoother with lambda=1600 on quarterly data has an approximately 32-quarter, -3.065 dB cutoff; preserving that cutoff requires rescaling lambda when sampling period or difference order changes.

Sec. 26.5 (physical PDF pp. 1305-1306; printed pp. 1282-1283): the WH transfer function has s reciprocal pole pairs; choosing the s inside-unit-circle poles yields a stable, real, symmetric, double-sided impulse response that decays exponentially away from time zero.

Sec. 26.6 (physical PDF pp. 1306-1311; printed pp. 1283-1288): Tikhonov deconvolution solves x=(F^TF+lambda D^TD)^(-1)F^Ty; positive lambda reduces condition number and noise amplification but introduces bias and smoothing.

Sec. 26.6 (physical PDF pp. 1308-1311; printed pp. 1285-1288): a regularized basis expansion can be rewritten entirely through kernel values K(x,x'), yielding the representer form f(x)=sum_n K(x,x_n)a_n with a=(lambda I+K)^(-1)y.

pedagogy: A computational, derivation-led engineering text that repeatedly moves from a physical or specification-level problem to equations, transform or matrix structure, an explicit sample-processing algorithm, and numerical verification. Across the book, the same idea is deliberately cross-checked as a signal model, convolution or transform relation, pole-zero or state-space property, block diagram, implementation, and plot. Early chapters build intuition through aliasing, quantization, rotating-wheel, converter, and convolution demonstrations; the central design chapters make tradeoffs concrete through frequency specifications, windows, prototype mappings, noise-reduction ratio, delay, settling time, and implementation cost; the application chapters reuse those tools for audio, compression, wavelets, control, smoothing, finance, seasonal decomposition, sparse recovery, and compact neural-network examples. Proofs are constructive and are usually carried through to coefficients, recursions, or code rather than presented abstractly. Exercises range from derivations and hand calculations to substantial C/MATLAB implementations, listening tests, reproducibility studies, hardware timing, full filter designs, control case studies, and a Markowitz portfolio project; some later chapters embed their experiments in the prose instead of supplying long formal problem sets. Prerequisites accumulate from complex numbers, Fourier analysis, sampling, convolution, and z-transforms to linear algebra, probability and random processes, differential equations, optimization, and least squares. The source is unusually rich in exact parameters, benchmark datasets, and executable procedures, though historical DSP-chip details, financial context, and many legacy code/data links should be modernized when adapting it to a current course.

gems: Example 1.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 39-40; printed pp. 16-17): a 10 Hz sinusoid sampled at only 12 Hz reconstructs as -2 Hz, turning aliasing into a single memorable arithmetic reduction.
Example 1.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 42-43; printed pp. 19-20): five analog frequencies -7, -3, 1, 5, and 9 Hz produce exactly the same samples at fs=4 Hz.
Example 1.4.4 (physical PDF pp. 43-44; printed pp. 20-21): sampling 4+3cos(pi t)+2cos(2pi t)+cos(3pi t) at half its Nyquist rate collapses distinct components into 5+5cos(pi t).

Example 1.6.1 (physical PDF pp. 65-66; printed pp. 42-43): in a 12 kHz audio chain with 2 kHz retained bandwidth and an 80 dB image target, the staircase DAC supplies 14.4 dB at the nearest image, leaving 65.6 dB for the analog postfilter.

Example 2.1.1 (physical PDF pp. 88-89; printed pp. 65-66): a 44 kHz, 10 V audio converter constrained below 50 microvolts RMS quantization noise lands at 16 bits, 44 microvolts, 704 kbit/s, and about 96 dB dynamic range.

Example 2.4.6 (physical PDF pp. 109-111; printed pp. 86-88): 1000 simulated errors with Q=1 give sigma=0.287 against Q/sqrt(12)=0.289, then histogram and correlation plots test the assumptions rather than merely asserting them.

Example 2.5.1 (physical PDF pp. 114-116; printed pp. 91-93): a 0.75-LSB sinusoid quantizes into an odd-harmonic, square-wave-like pattern; triangular dither audibly and visibly replaces the spurs with featureless noise.

Secs. 3.4-3.5 (physical PDF pp. 132-140; printed pp. 109-117): a centered five-tap smoother becomes causal with a two-sample delay, and the text generalizes the trick into a quantitative tail-clipping method for stable anticausal systems.

Example 4.1.1 and following forms (physical PDF pp. 147-157; printed pp. 124-134): the same two short sequences are carried through every convolution representation to the shared result [1,3,3,5,3,7,4,3,3,0,1].

Sec. 4.3.4 (physical PDF pp. 184-188; printed pp. 161-165): a 100 ms audio delay at 44.1 kHz needs 4410 stored samples, making the advantage of rotating an address pointer instead of copying a delay line impossible to miss.

Sec. 5.6 mortgage example (physical PDF pp. 239-241; printed pp. 216-218): a $10,000 five-year loan at 6% becomes a recurrence solved several ways, including unilateral z transform, yielding a $193.33 monthly payment and $1,599.68 total interest.

Example 6.3.2 (physical PDF pp. 258-260; printed pp. 235-237): a pole radius of 0.97 predicts a 151.2-sample 1% settling duration; a 300-sample gated sinusoid is therefore almost all input-on and input-off transient.

Example 6.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 272-274; printed pp. 249-251): at fs=600 Hz, rejecting 60 Hz and all its harmonics becomes the compact ten-notch numerator 1-z^-10 with nearby poles controlling notch width.

Sec. 6.5 (physical PDF pp. 274-283; printed pp. 251-260): the proposed ideal room processor deconvolves the listening room and then convolves a concert hall response, immediately exposing both the promise and fragility of inverse filtering.

Sec. 7.7 (physical PDF pp. 333-339; printed pp. 310-316): historical DSP32C cycle counts turn structures into hard sampling-rate limits—for example, a 100-tap FIR reaches roughly 112.4 kHz—providing a reusable real-time budgeting exercise even though the chip is obsolete.

Computer Experiments 8.10 (physical PDF pp. 378-383; printed pp. 355-360): a fourth-order double resonator becomes unstable when its direct coefficients are rounded to two digits while the cascade survives; a sixth-order Chebyshev direct form fails at four fractional digits while cascade and normalized lattice remain stable.

Example 9.2.1 (physical PDF pp. 397-398; printed pp. 374-375): a DTMF detector needs the DTFT at only eight frequencies, so selective evaluation/Goertzel beats a full FFT; the closest tone groups imply a minimum rectangular record of about 30 samples at 8 kHz.

Example 9.3.2 (physical PDF pp. 402-405; printed pp. 379-382): a middle sinusoid 60 dB below two strong neighbors is invisible under rectangular/Hamming leakage but recoverable with properly specified Kaiser, DPSS, or Chebyshev windows.

Sec. 9.7 (physical PDF pp. 425-426; printed pp. 402-403): the warning 'never accumulate or integrate white noise' is justified exactly by variance growing as (n+1)sigma_x^2, then repaired by one transparent pole-radius change.

Computer Experiment 9.8 (physical PDF pp. 426-431; printed pp. 403-408): 309 annual sunspot means from 1700-2008 expose the approximately 11-year cycle while ordinary, averaged, 50%-overlap Welch, and Bartlett-smoothed estimates make the resolution-variance tradeoff concrete.

A 5 kHz sinusoid sampled at 40 kHz for 128 samples cleanly separates the two meanings of resolution: the 312.5 Hz physical scale is fixed by the record, while a longer FFT merely fills in the displayed curve. [Example 10.3.1]

A 10 ms, 10 kHz sampled segment asks for 128 plotted frequencies only over 2.5–5 kHz, forcing the student to plan zero padding and bin selection from units rather than invoke an FFT mechanically. [Example 10.3.2]

The room-reverberation inverse problem models h(n)=Aa^n+Bb^n and identifies it from known input/output records by DFT-domain division—an unusually concrete bridge from fast convolution to system measurement. [Example 10.10.4]
The matched-filter computer experiment turns FFT multiplication into pulse detection/correlation, making the algorithmic chapter culminate in a recognizable signal-search task. [§10.13]
The Gibbs derivation lands on the memorable exact numerical overshoot Si(π)/π−1/2=0.08949 and explains why more taps move the error without shrinking its peak. [§11.2, Eq. 11.2.6]

Three audio crossover/equalizer designs escalate from a two-way loudspeaker split to three-way and then a five-band graphic equalizer, all exploiting complementary FIR responses and a shared pure delay. [Examples 11.3.3–11.3.5]

Three sinusoids at 2, 2.5, and 3 kHz include a middle component 50 dB down: Hamming’s approximately 40 dB sidelobe rejection hides it, whereas a 70 dB Kaiser design with length 193 reveals it. [Example 11.3.6]
Six parametric EQ filters at a 10 kHz rate put the center/bandwidth/gain formulas through a compact practical stress test rather than stopping with one abstract biquad. [Example 12.4.1]

The common-specification comparison requiring orders 35 (Butterworth), 10 (Chebyshev I), 10 (Chebyshev II), and only 5 (elliptic) is a striking quantitative argument for elliptic filters—and the paired phase plots show the price. [§13.1, Figs. 13.1.2–13.1.3]

For four-fold interpolation, the text calculates the missing samples X, Y, Z first by hold, then linear interpolation, then length-17 and length-25 FIR formulas using progressively more neighbors; typical CD filters use roughly 20–30 low-rate neighbors. [§14.1, Eqs. 14.1.1–14.1.3]

The delta-sigma table iterates a one-bit loop by hand for constant inputs 0.4 and −0.2; ten ±1 outputs average exactly to the respective input values, making pulse-density encoding immediately tangible. [Example 14.7.1]

A first-order one-bit delta-sigma ADC at 441 kHz recovers an 8.82 kHz sinusoid after 10-fold decimation; comparing an averager, length-21 rectangular FIR, and length-201 Kaiser FIR exposes accuracy versus delay. [Example 14.7.2]

The same example warns that a third-order shaper aiming at CD quality with L=64, 100 dB rejection, and Δf=0.1f_s would need about 4100 taps in a single-stage decimator—an unforgettable reason for multistage design. [Example 14.7.2]

The first Philips CD player is cited as using four-times oversampling and a first-order feedback requantizer, a concrete historical anchor for the chapter’s 'trade bits for samples' principle. [§14.7]

For smoothing a noisy constant, λ=0.90 gives n_eff=44, R=1/19, and 12.8 dB SNR gain, while λ=0.98 gives n_eff=228, R=1/99, and 20 dB: the benefit and settling penalty are visible in one pair of plots. [§15.2, Fig. 15.2.2]

The FIR-versus-EMA comparison is unusually decisive: at the EMA’s 44-sample settling time, an equal-length FIR has R=1/44 rather than 1/19; at equal R for λ=0.98, the FIR needs 99 taps versus the EMA’s 228-sample settling time. [§15.5, Fig. 15.5.1]

A 500 Hz sinusoid in unit-variance white noise, sampled at 10 kHz, is recovered with a radius-0.99 resonator; the example reports R≈1/99.6 and a 3.95-sample phase delay, keeping noise reduction and waveform shift in view together. [§15.4, Fig. 15.4.1]

The simulated ECG case shows why a 60 Hz single notch can fail: a period-10 square-wave contaminant also carries DC and odd harmonics. A Q=80 multi-notch filter removes the baseline and all replicated harmonics, while the single notch leaves most interference behind. [Examples 15.11.1–15.11.3]
A period-50 triangular signal buried in 50%-rms white noise is recovered by a Q=50 comb; R=0.0305 yields 15.16 dB SNR improvement and a 5.7× rms-noise reduction. [Example 15.11.5]

The video application translates a delay of D_H samples into the pixel directly above or below: line averaging separates luminance from alternating-phase chrominance but blurs vertical detail, which is then extracted from the difference channel and reinserted. [§15.12, Eqs. 15.12.26–15.12.35]

The DTMF example turns a keypad press into two parallel cosine resonators and then reverses the question at the receiver: recover one row frequency and one column frequency by an eight-filter bank or selected DFT bins. [§16.1.1, Example 16.1.1 and Figs. 16.1.3–16.1.4]

A simple echo and a simple reverberator differ only in which side of the delay is fed back, yet that small structural move changes a two-impulse FIR into an infinite, exponentially decaying room-like response. [§16.2.1, Figs. 16.2.2 and 16.2.6]
The chapter makes a memorable exception to ordinary DSP priorities: reverberation is valuable precisely for its transient, not its steady state. [§16.2.3]

The compressor section punctures the slogan that compression amplifies weak sounds: in the presented feedforward curve it attenuates only strong sounds, but the reduced overall dynamic range is perceived as if weak sounds grew. [§16.3.2, discussion after Figs. 16.3.3–16.3.4]

The ducker experiment uses speech as a side-chain to push music down only while someone talks, then asks the learner to tune attack, release, threshold, and ratio by listening rather than by a single numerical score. [§16.3.4, Experiment 2 and Eq. 16.3.15]

A five-iteration Landen implementation is enough for elliptic equalizer response error below 10^−5 percent, making the apparently exotic elliptic case only slightly more complicated than Chebyshev in practice. [§17.9, discussion after Fig. 17.9.4]

Changing equalizer gain in one jump produces overshoot, while as few as two intermediate gain steps largely remove it—a small control insight hidden inside an audio filter realization comparison. [§17.9, Fig. 17.9.7]

The phase-vocoder derivation explains phase unwrapping as measuring the deviation from the phase advance a DFT bin should have had, rather than as an arbitrary numerical cleanup. [§18.9, Eqs. 18.9.7–18.9.10]

The pitch-shift exercise asks for both listening evidence and spectral evidence on a flute, then traces a four-millisecond waveform through resampling, chipmunk playback, and duration restoration. [§18.11, Pitch-Scale Modification]
MDCT reconstruction is deliberately wrong block by block; exactness emerges only because adjacent wrong answers carry equal and opposite time-domain aliases. [§19.4, Eqs. 19.4.2–19.4.4]

The MDCT debugging table lists every overlapping IMDCT contribution for x=1,…,28; rows 5–24 add to exact integers even though the individual frame contributions look wildly aliased. [§19.6, MDCT/TDAC experiment]

The same four bumps/blocks/HeaviSine/Doppler signals appear in both the wavelet and local-polynomial chapters, creating a rare within-book head-to-head comparison rather than isolated success plots. [§20.7, Fig. 20.7.1; §23.19, Figs. 23.19.1–23.19.4]

A single eight-sample vector is carried through matrix DWT, convolutional DWT, multiple software packages, and exact inverse reconstruction; the differing sign/order conventions make implementation equivalence visible instead of hand-waved. [§20.5]

ZOH, forward Euler, FOH, trapezoidal integration, step invariance, and ramp invariance are shown as different faces of the same sampled-system construction rather than a list of unrelated recipes. [§§21.14–21.17]

The initial-condition mapping explains a subtle discontinuity: a causal input step can make y(0+) differ from y(0−) whenever the transfer function has direct feedthrough, even though the system itself is finite and causal. [§21.2, Eq. 21.2.1]

The control chapter escalates gracefully from car speed to radar antenna to inverted pendulum to bang-bang home heating, moving from clean linear transfer functions to a nonlinear simulation without changing the feedback story. [§22.4]

Local polynomial filters are presented as a recurring rediscovery: Schiaparelli in 1866, De Forest in 1871, actuarial graduation, Savitzky–Golay spectroscopy, and Henderson economic trend filters all solve closely related projection problems. [§23.1]

Polynomial preservation becomes peak preservation: the moment constraints retain area, centroid, and width information, which explains why Savitzky–Golay smoothing can protect narrow spectroscopic or ECG features better than a same-length averager. [§23.8, Eq. 23.8.16]

The ethanol example refuses to worship an automatic optimum: GCV chooses a visibly jagged fit, and the text recommends a nearby, slightly larger bandwidth based on judgment because the GCV minimum is broad. [§23.18, Figs. 23.18.4–23.18.5]

The motorcycle dataset contains 133 records but only 94 unique times; averaging repeats is not merely a shortcut, because weighting each average by its multiplicity is algebraically identical to fitting every observation. [§23.20, Eqs. 23.20.1–23.20.3]

Sec. 24.1 (physical PDF pp. 1186-1188; printed pp. 1163-1165): the running mean and EMA differ by only their gain schedule—one tends to zero and becomes unable to follow regime change, while the other stays finite and deliberately sacrifices consistency for tracking.

Example 24.5.1 (physical PDF pp. 1202-1204; printed pp. 1179-1181): a d=1 EMA and equivalent zero-lag FIR follow a noiseless piecewise-linear signal almost perfectly, then the same plots reveal their very different behavior after white noise is added.

Example 24.10.1 (physical PDF pp. 1218-1219; printed pp. 1195-1196): double EMA with lambda=0.8 and 0.9 develops peaks at periods of 42 and 86 samples, a concrete warning that a causal zero-lag smoother can amplify slow oscillations.

Sec. 25.3 (physical PDF pp. 1235-1237; printed pp. 1212-1214): SMA and linearly weighted WMA are not ad hoc formulas; both fall out of the same optimum predictive-filter family at two negative prediction distances.

Sec. 25.7 (physical PDF pp. 1253-1254; printed pp. 1230-1231): on the same 20-day Nicor Gas record, the SMA lag is 9.5 days while order-2 and order-3 Butterworth smoothers have lags 4.46 and 6.31 days, making structure-versus-delay tangible.

Secs. 25.9-25.10 (physical PDF pp. 1260-1265; printed pp. 1237-1242): the text places the familiar trader's zigzag beside L0 sparse trend filtering, then explicitly warns that extrapolating the last leg is risky because a future point can turn the endpoint into a kink.

Sec. 25.11 parabolic SAR example (physical PDF pp. 1270-1274; printed pp. 1247-1251): exact reversal days 9, 15, and 27 show the candidate stop, crossing event, and reset to the prior trend's extreme—an unusually clear nonlinear-state-machine case study.

Sec. 25.14 (physical PDF pp. 1282-1293; printed pp. 1259-1270): one computer project derives the efficient frontier, no-short-sale convex program, two-fund theorem, capital asset line, Sharpe ratio, security market line, CAPM, and LCMV generalization from a single quadratic form.

Example 26.2.1 (physical PDF pp. 1299-1300; printed pp. 1276-1277): monthly Easter Island–Darwin pressure differences reveal three cycles at 12, 26, and 44 months; WH smoothing and rank-6 SVD enhancement are compared against the NIST nonlinear fit in time and frequency.

Example 26.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 1304-1305; printed pp. 1281-1282): quarterly U.S. private-investment GDP from 1947–2008 is decomposed into trend and business cycle with the canonical lambda=1600 Hodrick-Prescott filter and checked against order-3 WH and rank-1 SVD alternatives.

Sec. 26.6 (physical PDF p. 1308; printed p. 1285): an ill-conditioned normal matrix with eigenvalues 10^-3 and 10^3 has condition number 10^6; adding lambda=10^2,10^3,10^4 cuts it to roughly 11,2,1.1 while progressively biasing the answer.

Example 26.9.1 (physical PDF pp. 1334-1337; printed pp. 1311-1314): sparse spike deconvolution gives about 26% error with L1 but only 0.52% with the L0 IRLS experiment, while ordinary inverse filtering magnifies stopband noise.

Example 26.9.2 (physical PDF pp. 1337-1341; printed pp. 1314-1318): recovering 100 nonzeros in a 2000-vector from 1000 noisy measurements yields 71.21% error for L2, 2.54% for L1, and 0.63% for L0 IRLS.

Example 27.2.2 (physical PDF pp. 1347-1349; printed pp. 1324-1326): a two-beat synthetic ECG sampled at 600 Hz is corrupted by 60 Hz harmonics and cleaned by a D=10 notch filter; its 40-dB transient lasts 732 samples, explaining the visibly delayed cleanup.

Example 27.7.2 (physical PDF pp. 1370-1374; printed pp. 1347-1351): monthly global CO2 from 1980–2009 is separated into smooth growth and annual seasonality; removing the trend makes the harmonic comb emerge clearly in the residual spectrum.

Example 27.9.2 (physical PDF pp. 1383-1385; printed pp. 1360-1362): a simplified X-11 implementation on 1980–2008 U.S. male unemployment closely reproduces the Bureau of Labor Statistics' independently published seasonally adjusted series.

Sec. 28.4.1 (physical PDF pp. 1405-1407; printed pp. 1382-1384): a 3:3:2 network learns all eight 3-bit parity patterns to outputs near 0.01/0.99; side-by-side sigmoid/tanh and pattern/epoch curves make initialization and convergence sensitivity explicit.

Sec. 28.4.3 (physical PDF pp. 1408-1411; printed pp. 1385-1388): a 4:4:1 network trains on 250 sunspot patterns and predicts the remaining 46, with the whiteness of training residuals checked through 45 autocorrelation lags.

Appendix A.3 (physical PDF pp. 1422-1426; printed pp. 1399-1403): Voss pink noise is built from held random streams at octave periods 1,2,4,...; the construction itself explains equal energy per octave and why the lowest credible frequency is fs/2^B.

Example B.1 (physical PDF pp. 1447-1449; printed pp. 1424-1426): for c=6 the Shannon number is 3.8197, and the tabulated PSWF eigenvalues fall from 0.9999, 0.9961, 0.9402, 0.6468 to 0.2073 and then rapidly toward 10^-14.
